stories.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
summary: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon.
The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

stories.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
summary: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

stories.title: What are heat pumps and how much do they cost?
summary: The government wants more homes to have heat pumps to cut fossil fuel use and drive down energy bills.

stories.title: Wildlife conservation cash targets ex-colliery sites
summary: The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards at sites in Yorkshire.

stories.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
summary: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material.
These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.

stories.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
summary: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree.
The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

stories.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy.
In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss.
Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

summary: Ten charges involved oil, cyanide and other pollutants entering local waterways.

stories.title: Rare rhino's first steps captured on video at zoo
summary: Zookeepers say the rhino's birth is a "special moment" for the under-threat one horned species.

stories.title: Wading bird called Phil tracked in epic migration to Siberia and back
summary: A bird has astonished conservationists by completing a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia and back.

stories.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks.

Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin.
Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

stories.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
summary: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal.

Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death.
Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.

stories.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership.
The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large.
Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

stories.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air.
Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

stories.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
summary: Survivors reject relocation plans they say ignore their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
